what_this_is: One serve cycle of the Go scheduler, captured from the old executable while it still runs, as the typed Registry effect it leaves behind. The C# scheduler must reproduce every field here from the same seeded fixture Home.

source.installed_by: fern-scheduler-cs install-scheduler-service, the ported C# installer, into a temporary deployment root
source.note: Go's own VerifyInstallation ran before its first Registry read and accepted the receipt the C# installer wrote. That is the old executable witnessing the install-gate port.

fixture.registry_home: built by the production migration chain through the digest-fixed fern-home; 56 migrations applied, zero scheduler leases

normalisation.serve_actor: <serve-actor>: the officer names itself with its own executable and pid; Go says fern-scheduler:serve:<pid> and C# says fern-scheduler-cs:serve:<pid>. Only the actor kind is compared.
normalisation.identifiers: <id> for a minted 32-hex identifier, <digest> for a 64-hex digest
normalisation.clock: <ms> for a Unix-millisecond reading, <time> for an ISO timestamp
normalisation.intervals: A dispatch block keeps retry_at_ms - blocked_at_ms, which is a declared interval and not a clock reading.

unproven_seam: A successful Plan claim and worker spawn. acquireChild hands off to the real fern-worker, a different executable and a different slice; here the worker is an identity probe, so the dispatch path ends in its durable refusal. The real claim and spawn are proved by the card Demo gate on local-4070, not by this golden.

dispatching.go_stdout: scheduler idle for <ms> ms; releasing office

plan_dispatch_blocks.reason: prepare-plan-child returned invalid JSON: json: unknown field "role"

declared_differences.difference: The block records why the dispatch failed, in the failing implementation's own words. Go says its worker returned invalid JSON; C# names its own refusal. Compared as non-empty, not verbatim.

Go asks a worker subprocess (prepare-plan-child) to claim the Plan and hand back a permit, so a worker that cannot answer leaves zero Attempts. C# claims the Plan in this process through the Registry writer and then spawns the supervisor directly; there is no hand-off subprocess. The card scope declares that design. So the dispatching case compares the observation half exactly and the claim half by contract: no accepted work is lost, and a Plan that cannot run leaves one durable dispatch block naming scheduler-serve:dispatch.
Each officer names itself with its own executable and pid. Normalised to <serve-actor>; the actor kind is compared instead.

Go blocks at scheduler-serve:dispatch, where its worker subprocess refused the hand-off. C# claims the Plan itself and spawns the supervisor, so its block arrives one cycle later from scheduler-serve:supervision, when that child exits non-zero. Both are one durable block on the same Plan with the same retry interval; the prefix is compared, the stage is not.

declared_differences.field: accepted_results.accepted_at and the acceptance receipt that repeats it
declared_differences.difference: Both write Go's RFC3339Nano shape: UTC, trailing Z, fractional zeros trimmed. The remaining difference is clock resolution, not format: Go offers nanoseconds and .NET hundreds of nanoseconds, so C# never writes the last two digits. Normalised to <time>.
